title: Making make-up in Ancient Egypt
authors: Walter P., Martinetto P., Tsoucaris G., Brniaux R., Lefebvre M.A., Richard G., Talabot J., Dooryhee E.

Use open copies via Unpaywall/Crossref, repositories, or PMC.
quote: laurionite and phosgenite appear to be synthetic products manufactured by the Egyptians using ‘wet’ chemistry
summary: Quantitative crystallographic and chemical analysis of cosmetic powders dated c. 2000-1200 BC found galena and cerussite plus laurionite and phosgenite, which the authors read as deliberately synthesised lead compounds.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened (the rest is a paywall preview); methods, sample numbers and the synthesis experiments were not read. 'Appear to be' is an inference from the absence of natural or ageing origins. Later work (Riesmeier 2022) still words it as 'likely'.

title: Recipes of Ancient Egyptian kohls more diverse than previously thought
authors: Riesmeier M., Keute J., Veall M.-A., Borschneck D., Stevenson A., Garnett A., Williams A., Ragan M., Devièse T.
ask_addressed: Open the primary analytical papers behind Khemet's chemical crafts: Walter et al. 1999 (Nature), Rehren and Pusch 2005 (Science), Kovalev et al. 2023 (JAS), Hatton Shortland Tite 2008, Odler on copper, Buckley and Evershed 2001 and 2004 full text. Use open copies via Unpaywall/Crossref, repositories, or PMC.
quote: The presence of laurionite and phosgenite in Ancient Egyptian make-up likely stems from synthetic manufacture
summary: Multi-analytical study (FTIR, GC-MS, XRD and others) of 11 Petrie Museum kohl containers: lead compounds are not the only inorganic ingredient, organic components are common, and laurionite/phosgenite turn up in some samples, cited to Walter 1999.
limits: Open access copy of the main follow-up to Walter 1999 and shows its finding is confined to a few samples out of 11. It broadens, and so partly qualifies, the older view of kohl as a lead-only product. Provenance and dating of some containers is loose.

quote: The identification of non-local organic substances enables the reconstruction of trade networks that provided ancient Egyptian embalmers with the substances required for mummification
summary: GC-MS of 31 labelled vessels from a 26th Dynasty embalming workshop at Saqqara links Egyptian names (antiu, sefet) to oil, tar and resin mixtures, and shows imported materials (Pistacia, conifer by-products, dammar, elemi).
limits: A single late (26th Dynasty) workshop, so it does not by itself describe Old or New Kingdom practice. Open-access full text, read via Europe PMC.

summary: GC-MS, HT-GC-MS and LC-MS/MS of balm residues from canopic jars of the 18th Dynasty noble lady Senetnay (c. 1450 BCE, KV42) found beeswax, plant oil, fats, bitumen, Pinaceae resins and dammar or Pistacia resin.

summary: SEM-EDS, XRF, multispectral imaging and Raman imaging of Egyptian blue from New Kingdom shabtis at Deir el-Medina show compositional variation (two possible production groups) and luminescing versus non-luminescing silicate phases.

title: Source of Raw Materials and Its Processing for the Manufacturing of Ptolemaic Faience Bowls from Tell Atrib (Nile Delta, Egypt)
authors: Trzciński J., Zaremba M., Nejbert K., Kaproń G.
ask_addressed: Quote findings and limits. Add any open text on Egyptian faience production and on gold metallurgy.
quote: The basic raw material used for the manufacturing of faience artefacts in ancient Egypt was silica
summary: Petrographic and image analysis of quartz grains in Ptolemaic faience bowls from Athribis traces the quartz to Eastern Desert gold-bearing vein sources and reconstructs crushing and grinding stages.
limits: Ptolemaic period, so it speaks to late faience, not Pharaonic origins of the craft. The Eastern Desert provenance is an inference from grain character.

title: Gold and Silver: Relative Values in the Ancient Past

summary: Documents more than 200 relative gold and silver values (2500 BCE-400 CE) and concludes that supply mattered more than purity; Nubian gold access shaped the gold:silver ratio in Egypt and the Near East until about 1100 BCE.
